reason: The audit itself is correct. watch.log l.3-5 shows three events: 04:13:06Z exp70a 0.954 NEU, 04:31:08Z exp70e 0.949 NEG and 04:56:17Z exp70d 0.949 NEG. D1-3 gives {#37, #38}. The only action proposed, the wording fix, is wrong on mechanism, so the finding is refuted. With J = TP/(TP+FP+FN), removing a fork of precision q changes J by about (-q + (1-q)J)/D, so the break-even is q* = J/(1+J). A HIGHER public J (~0.36, q* 0.265) versus the lab (0.129, q* 0.114; 0.192/0.161 on the K2 stack) makes removals MORE tolerable on public at a fixed precision. It therefore cannot explain why dc0.30 cost -0.005 on public while the lab showed +0.0013. The flip comes from the precision of the removed forks. The lab 6bba removed 0 TP and 6 FP (q ~0). On public, 20 of 75 dummy forks were removed for -0.004 to -0.006, which implies q well above 0.265. This is what the CONTEXT 04:59Z entry already says: the true divisions sit in DC bands the lab does not predict. The original line 'the lab sign was wrong for this knob' is literally true. The R15 recheck verdict (3) relies on it: a division-knob sign comes from the public LB or from nothing. Softening it weakens a valid caution. The rewrite would also edit a dated record after the fact, and its 'public DC gain carries over weakly' does not follow from the break-even argument. For fork ADDITIONS, a lower private q* makes transfer easier. The weak-transfer case rests on precision/shift (lab dc0.20: +6 FP, 0 TP), not on J.
